title: Confucian self-cultivation
hook: Confucians work on themselves to bring order to home and world (Great Learning)

segments.voice: Yesterday, li: ritual and courtesy, the form that trains the heart from the outside in. Your line was courtesy shapes. Did the courtesy you rehearsed shift anything when you did it? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

In a kitchen cupboard sits a set of nesting bowls. The big one holds the middle one, which holds the small one, which holds the smallest, right at the center. Each bowl sits inside the next. Now a different scene. The news is loud. Something is wrong in the world, and something is wrong in your town, and at home there's a sharp word from this morning still hanging in the kitchen. Where do you even start? An old Confucian text, the Great Learning, answers that question with something like those nesting bowls, and it names the one to start with.
screen: `NESTING BOWLS.` → `THE WORLD, THE TOWN, THE KITCHEN.` → `WHERE DO YOU START?`

segments.voice: The Great Learning is a short text, and its opening is a chain. It speaks of the ancients who wanted bright virtue to shine through the whole realm. To do that, it says, they first ordered their own states. To order their states, they first set their families right. And then the line at the heart of it, in Legge's translation: "Wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons." The chain keeps going inward. To cultivate themselves, they made their hearts right. To make their hearts right, they made their thoughts sincere. To make their thoughts sincere, they extended their knowledge, by looking closely at things. Then the text turns around and runs the chain outward again: when things are looked into, knowledge is complete; then thoughts become sincere; hearts become right; the self is cultivated; the family is in order; the state is well governed; and the whole realm is at peace. The Chinese term at the center is xiushen, cultivating the self. Cultivate is a farming word in English, and it fits: not a makeover, but slow, daily tending, like a garden. Notice what the Great Learning doesn't say. It doesn't say ignore the world. The goal is still peace for everyone. But it insists the work starts at the smallest bowl. The text then says, in paraphrase, that from the ruler down to ordinary people, cultivating the self is the root of everything else, and when the root is in disorder, what grows from it can't be in order. For a Confucian, then, fixing yourself is not selfish. It's the first, and nearest, piece of fixing the world.
screen: `STATE, FAMILY, SELF: THE CHAIN GOES IN.` · `HEART, THOUGHTS, KNOWLEDGE.` · `THEN IT RUNS OUTWARD TO PEACE.` · `XIUSHEN: TENDING THE SELF LIKE A GARDEN.` · then, large: `THEY FIRST CULTIVATED THEIR PERSONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put one small thing in order. Settle, and breathe. Let your attention come to the smallest bowl: you. Ask quietly: what is one small thing in my own life that's out of order right now? A cluttered corner. A reply I owe. A habit slipping. A grudge I keep feeding. Don't choose the biggest one. Choose one small enough to fix today. Hold it in mind, and picture it put right. Breathe in, and see it done. Breathe out, and let the rest wait its turn. The bell holds the time.
Confucian self-cultivation. Xiushen: tending your own heart, thoughts and conduct, as the root from which order in the family and the world can grow. Today's word.

Your line: start with me. Today, put that one small thing in order, before you try to fix anything bigger. Then notice whether anything around it settles a little. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Students of the Confucian tradition read and memorize the Great Learning and treat self-cultivation, through study, reflection, sincere intention and right conduct, as the starting point for good family life and good government.

myth: the Great Learning tells people to ignore the world and fix themselves
the goal is still peace for the whole realm. it says the work starts with the self.
the chain runs inward, then outward again
state, family, self, heart, thoughts, knowledge; then back out to peace in the whole realm.
self-cultivation is only for rulers, in this text
it says, from the ruler down to ordinary people, cultivating the self is the root.

fork.setup: you want peace in your family. by the Great Learning's chain, where do you begin?
fork.reveal: "wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons." the chain puts the self beneath the family.

original.note: Chinese, from the Great Learning: to cultivate the self.

trapdoor: what you thought: self-cultivation sounds like self-improvement for your own sake.
what it means: tending your heart and conduct as the root from which order in home and world can grow.
what a scholar hears: the Great Learning's chain, running inward from the realm to the investigation of things, then outward to peace.

sources.quoted: Wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons.

sources.ref: The Great Learning, opening text (the full chain, and cultivation of the person as the root)

notes: The Great Learning line is quoted from Legge 1861 from memory; verify exact wording. The rest of the chain and the 'root' passage (自天子以至於庶人，壹是皆以修身為本) are paraphrased.
'Cultivate is a farming word in English' is a remark about the English word, not an etymology of xiushen; cut if the editor prefers.
The nesting-bowls opening is an everyday image, not a claim about a tradition.
'From the ruler down to ordinary people' paraphrases 'from the Son of Heaven down to the mass of the people'. Confirm.

Editor pass: the hook's bowl image was garbled (pulling out the smallest nested bowl doesn't make a stack wobble, and the smallest sits at the center, not the bottom); it now says each bowl sits inside the next and the text 'names the one to start with'. The carry's 'stack wobbles' line was changed to match. Legge's chain line checked.
